LIMBO is a grim platformer in which you journey through an eerie world full of darkened enemies to reunite with your sister. In terms of a story, that's about all you get. Rather, the strength of this game is its atmopshere, puzzles, and some aspects of exploration.

You're given no real context about who or where you are, creating a mysterious tone that endures throughout the game. The art direction complements this perfectly. At no point do you have to wait through loading screens; the world is designed very fluidly, with each area leading smoothly into the next. While the levels are mostly linear, you are expected to backtrack in several; the game encourages exploration, with side paths often leading to hidden rewards.

The controls are extremely simple, relying only on the arrow keys and Ctrl by default. The puzzles start out relatively straightforward, but progressively increase in both difficulty and complexity as you continue. With every successive level, you are introduced to a new mechanic or aspect of level design that enhances the traps. While the overall theme of the game is relatively somber, the more exciting areas require quick thinking and precise movements. Many of the later puzzles involve quite a bit of trial and error, but I never became overly frustrated with any of them.

The only issues I have with the game are that it is locked to 60fps in fullscreen mode, and that the controls cannot be changed from the in-game menu. However, these things are not especially problematic. All things considered, the atmosphere and puzzles are fascinating. It's well worth a playthrough, especially if you can get it on sale.

Played the game a few years ago and finally decided to come back and get the last achievement recently.  The first run may take a few hours and experienced players can finish within a hour.  Overall a good indie and recommended to play.

To complete the game in one sitting with no more than 5 deaths is not easy but very doable after some practice.  It’s essential to know how to solve each puzzle quickly and save death counts for those areas require accurate timings.  Using chapter select to practise difficult areas can be very helpful.

Even after all these years, LIMBO is still one of the greatest indie-game. It's hard to classify it: it's a platformer, but it will rarely require good timing; it's a puzzle game, but you won't spend hours trying to figure out solutions; it's a horror game, but there's no blood, no jumpscare, not even fear, just a disturbing atmosphere. 

I wouldn't recommend this game if someone asked me to suggest a platformer, a puzzle game or a horror game. But for someone asking for something new and/or looking for a game with a peculiar atmosphere, I wouldn't hesitate one second. PLAY THIS GAME!

One of the strangest game I've played in years this one! When you hear the title of this game, you think it could be a party game. Instead, it really is a dark, horrifying platformer, where you have to guide a cute little boy through the dark world called Limbo: A place between heaven and hell. At least that is what has been told. 

In fact, there is no storyline at all. All that you know is that the boy wakes up in a dark forest, and has to make it's way to the end.
It will not be an easy walkover, though: The further you get, the harder it will become. The boy will easily fall victim to a cruel and painful death.

Overall: Limbo offers a variety of incredible puzzles, outstanding visual/sound design, and an immersive world that you will not want to come out of.
If you would like to play an original, challenging platformer, Limbo is surely recommendable.

Limbo does not have an elaborate storyline. The game takes place in a forest that is on the edge of hell, a piece of no man's land. You play a boy who suddenly wakes up, as if he has been unconscious for a while. His last memory is of his sister, who is nowhere to be seen. Despite the grim, gray and dark atmosphere that prevails in the forest, he is determined to find his sister.

Watch a short gameplay of Limbo here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ceibXirZ29I

Limbo is a two-dimensional platformer with very simple controls. You can walk, jump, push crates and other objects and climb ropes and ladders. So don't try to swim in one of the many lakes you come across.
To progress in the game you have to solve various puzzles. The puzzles vary widely: from defusing bear traps to crossing a river, from reaching higher plateaus to operating machines correctly. Most puzzles in the beginning are a piece of cake. As you progress through the game, the more difficult the puzzles become.

The game is also great on a steam deck: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5R71bhdH4bM

With most puzzles it is a matter of trial and error, or “trial and death” as the game Danish developers call it. You try to solve a puzzle, but find yourself not doing it quite right, so you try again.
Once you have solved a puzzle and hit the next obstacle, your progress will be saved. So you don't have to worry about ending up very far back in the game and having to redo entire parts. If you don't feel like playing any further in the middle of the game, then continue from that point next time.
Crates, tires, bear traps, boats, corpses, machines, magnets: you can think of it so crazy or you can use it to solve puzzles. Some obstacles even require you to use gravity. All in all, Limbo contains many fun, challenging and ingenious puzzles.

The graphics with carefully chosen background music create a dark and ghostly atmosphere, exactly what Limbo wants to achieve.

A game that is underrated by some, loved by majority and appreciated only by true puzzle-platformer enthusiast.

Once it gets a hold of you, it is truly impossible to break free from its tight grip that squeezes every juices of your brain as you keep moving forward to the unknown. The danger that lurks within causes you inevitable horrifying gruesome painful death. And yes, death is not a flat straight one but rather this game will let you experience variety of ways you could die in different forms and circumstances. Not every death is the same as you advance forward through this game. Death is truly handled in such cold manner that keeps me shocked and entertained simultaneously even after I saw it a dozen of times.

I love the ever challenging hurdles, how it was cleverly and uniquely executed. The story was intentionally left ambiguous, full of mysteries and symbolism, leaving me hanging even after I finished the game.

Minimalist yet haunting. Smart puzzles, tight controls, and a chilling atmosphere that sticks with you after the credits. Short but memorable. A must-play if you appreciate mood and design over dialogue.

Limbo is for me, truly original piece of art. Dark, harsh tone, black and white gore, and challenging puzzles are major pluses. Other thing i adore, is vizualization itself. I felt that, sometimes are just too hard, especially when i was closer to the end. Some people find this type of challenge great, but at some point, i was discouraged to finish this game. In the end i really enjoy playing this game, it was different type of joy, depressive joy i could say.

Limbo is a timeless indie masterpiece that redefined the puzzle-platformer genre with its minimalist yet deeply atmospheric approach. Developed by Playdead, the game immerses players in a haunting monochromatic world filled with mystery and danger.

The striking black-and-white visuals, combined with a chillingly minimalist sound design, create an eerie and unsettling atmosphere that grips you from start to finish. The puzzles are clever, intuitive, and seamlessly tied to the environment, offering just the right balance of challenge and satisfaction.

What makes Limbo stand out is its ability to tell a profound, thought-provoking story without a single word of dialogue. Its themes of survival, loss, and exploration resonate deeply, making it more than just a game, it's an experience.

For fans of atmospheric and emotionally driven games, Limbo is an absolute must-play. Its influence on the indie game scene is undeniable, and its haunting world will stay with you long after you’ve reached the end.

Playdead games strikes gold with the hit title LIMBO. LIMBO is a game which keeps you guessing with interesting puzzles, complex scenarios, and an intriguing story. The games artistic styling’s does not seem cheap, but rather creates an ambience that makes LIMBO seem rather elegant. 

[b]Summary:[/b]
LIMBO is a side scroller where you play a young boy who is on an adventure to seek his missing sister. The game is a platform game with integrated puzzles to solve in order to progress through to the next part of the game. The grey-tone of the game creates a rather fearful and discerning environment where a gruesome fate looks poetic. The game gets progressively harder and the puzzles become more challenging as you progress, although once you get a hang of the game you'll figure out it’s not too difficult. You meet many challenges along the way from rising water levels, monsters that force you in a direction, rope swinging, traps, and more that keep you on your toes. LIMBO is a great game which offers fantastic yet horrific scenery, music, and ambience. The game keeps you on your toes and the clever grayscale art style allows a rather terrifying world to be poetic. 

[b]Controls:[/b]
My major gripe about this game was the control system. Although, I write a lot about this, it is actually a rather minuscule problem and doesn't at all ruin the games experience. You cannot edit the controls from inside the game, because the developers decided not to allow key-mapping within the games interface you must exit the game and edit the settings file within the LIMBO steamapps folder. The controls are worse because the jump command which is listed in the settings file is not an actual command in the game; there are only five commands: Left, Right, Up, Down, and Use. There are no resolution settings, so if you are using an odd resolution you may have problems playing this game. The one complaint I have towards this game is that character doesn't always respond well to the controls, which causes a lot of deaths that could easily be avoided if the character control system was better. 

[b]Gameplay Hints:[/b]
[spoiler]>When you get a brain slug running under the light allows you to turn the other direction.
>The "up" key (mine was W) is not a jump key, it moves you up and coincidently this means you jump with it. When gravity field reverses you must use the "down" key (S) rather than "up" key (W) to jump as you are moving down. 
>Do not hold the "up" key while on a rope as if you do clicking the "left" or "right" key will jump you off the rope. If you are not holding the "up" key then you will just swing left and right gaining momentum.[/spoiler]

[b]Results:[/b]
Overall this game is a fun, the puzzles are challenging, difficulty curve is smooth, scenery is fabulous, ambience is frighteningly amazing, gameplay is elegant, and the symbolism makes the story phenomenal. I would completely recommend this game. [b]I purchased it at a discount, but if I knew it was this fun I would have paid full price.[/b]

[h2]Once upon a time: an effort for nothing![/h2]

The boy is unconscious on the ground. He slowly opens his eyes with great pain. He gets up and finds himself in a big forest. A forest that a boy so small is afraid of. But the boy overcomes fear. Because he has to find his sister…

[h2]Black, white, thousands of colors![/h2]

Nothing can be said in praise of the graphics of this wonderful game. The creators of this game have created thousands of colors and images using white and black. The player in all places of the game praises the stunning graphics and the high accuracy of the creators in the design of the environment and objects. In fact, the environment is painted with thousands of shadows and lights, and this has caused a great increase in the beauty of the artistic graphics of this game. In fact, the creators have done a great job and have used thousands of different black and white colors. So that you feel that the whole environment of the game is painted and each color is different from the other. The design of objects in the game is also really wonderful. So that you are surprised by all this precision. From making gears and light bulbs to making a giant spider. An important point has been observed in all of these, that is, quality and accuracy! So I tell you that you will not feel any shortage in the graphics of this game. But in some places the graphics could be stronger.

[h2]Silence is the greatest music[/h2]

The sounding of this title has been done in a very precise manner and in accordance with the principles. Before dealing with the music of the game, it is necessary to mention the sounds of the objects, movement and various events of the game. From the foot of the spider sinking into the boy's body to the sound of him running on the ground, it is set so precisely that it makes the environment and atmosphere of the game more believable for the player. The sound of the rustling of the wind and the falling and rolling of a stone on the mountain is no different from the real sound of this happening in life and in the real world. It's as if the creators have made a giant spider for sound and stuck its sharp leg in a boy's body and recorded this sound and put it on their game

[h2]And the soundtrack:[/h2]

In this sector as well, Playdead has been quite successful. It is true that in many scenes silence is the only music of the game, but... but it must be admitted that this silence in the game is wonderful. Silence, next to which real sounds can be heard from the environment of a terrible forest. The silence that multiplies stress and fear in the game. A silence that should really be praised. Of course, the game in its special and emotional parts also has music that is completely in harmony with the events and makes the story more interesting.

[h2]Alone in the forest[/h2]

One of the most important parts of a game is its gameplay. No matter how great the music, graphics and story of the game are, if the gameplay of that game does not complete the rest, we will definitely face a weak title. But it must be said that this title has not left anything short for the players in this section as well.

What do you expect from the gameplay of a platformer title? If in your opinion, the great gameplay of a platformer title should be full of puzzles and different tasks, and you are supposed to face the biggest enemies in the game with simple methods and experience all kinds of vehicles in a very simple but beautiful game, and in general Never get tired of playing that title, I have to tell you that Limbo has a great gameplay.

In this game, there are no options on the game screen. In fact, you and the up, down, left and right buttons and a button to interact with the environment! There is no amount of life or... in the game, and as it was said, the game environment is completely free of any pictures or signs or writings. It is as if you are sitting in front of an animation screen. In the game you have only 2 modes, alive or dead. There is no middle ground. One mistake will kill you, and doing a simple task correctly will keep you alive, and it is not the case that, for example, your energy or life will decrease and you will be fine again! The game is completely real! Anything can cause death and death is really simple and real!

[h2]An effort for nothing[/h2]

We talked about all the parts of the game, but now we come to the biggest story of this game: its wonderful story. A story whose many parts are dumb for you. In fact, you and your belief must complete those parts of the game and complete the story. Limbo is made in such a way that everyone can make their own interpretation of it. But all perceptions are actually summed up in one concept. Something that only the player will understand after completing all the stages of the game.

Limbo literally means purgatory. The limbo in which this boy is caught. It's a terrible place for anyone…
The player is drowning in thoughts and questions. But the child overcomes the most difficult places. The boy tries his best. Finally, he uses magnetism. He does something difficult and the boy breaks the glass and is thrown in that direction. The boy is unconscious on the ground. Just like the first game...

Does the player get scared that I have been around myself all this time? What is going to happen to this little boy? The boy opens his eyes again in the same shot as the beginning of the game. He is in pain. He gets up and moves forward. It reaches the same tree house at the beginning of the game. The boy sees his sister crying over her dead body. Does this mean that this was a boy's torment? For what mistake is he tormented? This child who has not done anything to want to suffer in Purgatory. Did I mean something else? But the final message is clear:

The boy has been dead for a long time.
But there are still thousands of questions left in the mind. This game has literally destroyed the player in the story. Of course, the most painful message of the game is determined after the list of creators goes up and the game menu reappears.

Both the boy and his sister were dead.
Maybe many have not noticed this message, but if you look carefully, you will see flies flying above the 2 corpses under the tree house...

[h2]First:[/h2] The boy and his sister go to a tree house in a forest for fun or escape. The boy's sister goes out of the hut for some reason or for example to fetch something. The second theory is more likely to be true due to the evidence. Because at the end of the game, the girl sees the boy and gets up and runs away. How could he see a ghost if he wasn't dead? An independent platformer developed by a Danish company called Playdead. Limbo has a unique, eerie atmosphere that usually characterises the horror genre. The atmosphere is the result of the dark (black and white) presentation and the lack of music throughout the adventure.

It is one of those trial-and-error games where in order to successfully solve a puzzle in many cases you either need to react quickly or you have only one chance for a perfect execution. If you fail you can start all over from the previous checkpoint and you should also watch how the boy dies (often in quite a gruesome way). To be honest, I can easily imagine that this unique presentation deters some gamers from even trying out the game. Its trailer, in fact, presents the game's one-of-a-kind aesthetics very well.

There is a nice learning curve here and the game has some easter eggs for you to collect - mainly for the purpose of extra achievements, of course. If you love hardcore gaming you can complete Limbo in one sitting with fewer than 5 deaths to earn the hardest achievement of the game.

Limbo has a unique atmosphere. While it is not a long platformer it certainly is a great game. Unfortunately, due to its length and genre I consider 10 EUR a bit too expensive - still, we all know there are regular discounts so until it happens it deserves a place in everybody's wishlist.

Limbo is a fantastic atmospheric puzzle game, with beautiful visuals achieved through a monochrome colour scheme and an eerie soundscape that really immerses you in the world. 

The story itself is rather ambiguous but is fun to play and contemplate about nonetheless. 

Controls can be finicky at times, especially when you're adjusting to them at the beginning at the game and can be inconsistent within certain puzzles, but they are easy to get the hang of. 

It's very much a puzzle game that will require you to die a few times to figure out what you're doing/where you're going. The puzzles themselves aren't too difficult to solve, but as with every puzzle game there are going to be a select few where the solutions don't jump right out at you. This can occasionally lead to some annoyance, though as this is an old game now, if you're really stuck you can always look up a walkthrough. 

It's not your typical jumpscare horror, it builds up its scary and surreal atmosphere through visual, sound and story design, and these are its strongest elements. 

All in all, for the cheap price that it is, there's no reason why you shouldn't try this game if you're a fan of puzzle platformers/indie games. If you've played INSIDE and/or Little Nightmares as well, you're guaranteed to love it.

A cinematic masterpiece, this game never ceases to amaze me and fulfill that sudden desire for mysticism and minimalism that is so hard to achieve in gaming. The first time I played it was in 2013. It has spawned many pretenders since; those who seek to captivate its magic but seldom get it right. It was groundbreaking when it came out and it is groundbreaking today.

The premise is terrifying; to be a child in an apocalyptic setting where sadistic children are overlords is troubling enough, never mind the scenery, the music and the mood. You are pulled into this grotesque scenario where the world (and anything that moves, parasitic or otherwise) is your enemy but not as a machine gun-wielding, monster destructing, roid machine but rather as an innocent, vulnerable child who is about to be trampled by the darkness that surrounds him. Everything is dark and not just in color, but also intention. 

It’s as if the world were already lost. But the thing that makes this game different, I think, is that you are not trying to save it… no, far from it. The premise is survival in a very primal way. This game could play out in a few days real time and most of us wouldn’t realistically survive it, let alone electronically. Even though I finished it long ago, I still remember the ending. Perhaps too romantic for its own sake, it was a smile for a tragic journey, a gentleness from developers who made us suffer much along the way. This game is an experience and one that I’ll never totally recover from, nor do I want to. I will replay it again in 2019 and see how much I’ve grown since my first playthrough, how the memories compare. For now, it is time to set foot in the darkest plains of Limbo again. Good day, gentlemen.

Last night, I played through Limbo for the first time and took about 3 and half hours to complete it. Overall, I enjoyed my experience and found the game to be quite fun, especially in the first half of the game. I did have a few issues, but I'll go into further detail about that below. If you want to go into the game not knowing what to expect, I'd say buy it play through it now - it's pretty good. If you want to see my full thoughts on the game, however, then you can continue reading below - just be warned that it may spoil a few things for you.

Firstly, I need to say that the visuals and audio in this game is phenomenal. Just look at the screenshots of the game. They're beautiful. The colour palette is very simple with only black, white, and grey - but this simplicity is its strength, as it helps to create a very thematic and immersive atmosphere. The audio is amazing as well, both the music and the sound effects help to cultivate a somewhat eerie feeling and immerse you into the game (it's worth noting here that I played with headphones in, so that definitely helped the immersion factor). 

Adding to the atmosphere is the somewhat unsettling and disturbing imagery, and the variety of brutal deaths that can befall your character should you fail any section. You will die a lot - I certainly did. There's plenty of ways to die, form falling in pits, drowning, being impaled on spikes or cut up by saws. You can even be shot to pieces (literally) but machine guns later in the game. Plus there are numerous other ways to die. This is an especially strong aspect in the early game where you must avoid attacks from two distinct threats. First there's the spider which is suitably horrifying and scary as it persistently hunts you down to mercilessly impale you with its legs. There's also a bunch of other boys running around in the forest. They've built tree forts, placed traps along your path, and as you attempt to pass through, they'll even attack you directly with blowdarts. They have no qualms about killing, and you can find the corpses of other boys who have fallen victim to their traps. Another particularly horrifying threat are the glowing parasites that will latch onto your head a few times throughout the game. They take partial control over your movement, choosing the direction you face and forcing you to move - however you can still jump, and you get to control how fast you move (walking, running, etc). They are introduced when another boy walks straight into a lake and drowns right before your eyes. I thoroughly enjoyed this immersive and somewhat horrifying atmosphere, but I feel it fell a bit flat in the later half of the game, as you move away from the forest and into what appears to be some kind of urban area. In the later half of the game, the threats you face began more generic and less overtly terrifying. Saw blades, machinery, electrified surfaces. Though I admire the variety of threats in the game, these latter ones feel a little more boring than a giant spider and murderous boys. They also get a bit overused - especially saws. 

In terms of gameplay, Limbo is pretty fun. It has lots of platforming and quite a few puzzles. As the game progresses both of these elements get more challenging and harder - sometimes a little too hard I think. I made fairly even progress throughout the game - occasionally needing a few tries in some sections, but near the game's end there were a few sections in particular which were very frustrating. I think the main reason for this is the game relies on quick movements and precise timing in some sections. Admittedly this isn't exactly my cup of tea (I prefer to take my time) and some people may enjoy games with these sorts of challenges, but I found it annoying at many points. The problem usually isn't that you don't know what to do, but rather that doing it can be somewhat difficult. One of the worst examples is the bug (Ant? Wasp? Not sure exactly what it is) which you come across eating something on the ground. To progress you need to sneak up on it by moving, then stopping when it looks up to investigate the sound. It's a fairly straight forward section once you know what you've gotta do, but the tricky part is getting the timing and position right to jump at the bug and grab onto its leg as it flies away. If you move too close, it'll detect you and fly away. If you aren't close enough, you won't reach its leg and you'll have to back away and start over again. Getting the right timing took numerous attempts, and it was quite frustrating. There were a few other sections that gave me trouble, but if went into them all I'd be here all day, so moving on...

My final thoughts are still positive. I want to say again just how phenomenal the audio and visual elements of this game are. Though I stand by my belief that the game falters in the second half of the game, it still thinks its pretty good. Just bear in mind that it can be frustrating at times, and often relies on specific timing, so if that's something you don't enjoy or struggle with, I suggest you look elsewhere. If you're fine with this, then I'd definitely recommend the game. I would also suggest playing through with headphones of added immersion.

I'd also like to mention that there are hidden eggs that you can find throughout the game. I only got two (I think they're like eight or ten in total) but if you enjoy searching for that kind of stuff you can probably get a few more hours of gameplay out of this game.

[b]"Minimalist, Creepy, and Brilliantly Sad"[/b]

Limbo is a haunting journey through a monochrome world where every shadow seems to whisper secrets, and every step feels like a descent deeper into the unknown. From the moment you awaken in a dark forest, the game offers no hand-holding—no dialogue, no instructions, just the eerie soundscape and the boy's silhouette against the bleak backdrop. It's a minimalist approach that speaks volumes, drawing players into its enigmatic narrative .

The gameplay is a blend of platforming and puzzle-solving, with each section introducing new mechanics that challenge your perception and timing. The puzzles are cleverly designed, often requiring a mix of logic and experimentation. While some players have noted a shift towards trial-and-error in the latter half, the sense of accomplishment upon solving them is undeniable .

Visually, Limbo is a masterpiece. The black-and-white art style, combined with subtle animations and ambient lighting, creates an atmosphere that's both beautiful and unsettling. It's a world where danger lurks in every corner, and the line between life and death is blurred. The sparse sound design, punctuated by moments of silence and sudden noises, amplifies the tension, making every encounter feel significant .

However, the game's brevity—lasting around 3 to 4 hours—might leave some yearning for more. Yet, this concise experience ensures that every moment is impactful, and the story's ambiguity invites players to interpret its meaning long after the screen fades to black .

In essence, Limbo is more than just a game; it's an experience that lingers, prompting reflection on its themes of innocence, death, and the unknown. For those seeking a game that challenges both the mind and the emotions, Limbo stands as a testament to the power of minimalist storytelling in gaming.

Here also lies strength as the game is very good about little details and cues to warn you of potential dangers. Sound effects, lighting and random moving objects are used to teach a player without using words. There is even a secret level that is almost entirely done in darkness but it somehow works due to mentioned examples. The controls are easy to grasp and they’re responsive enough for this to not get in the way. The game is long enough to keep your attention and knows when to end things before it becomes repetitive. Like for instance not being able to tell there is a rope you can hold on to or a button you can press for a puzzle. 

Limbo is worthy of being a classic. I definitely recommend giving it a shot, especially with it often being on sale. If you approach LIMBO with an experiential and immersive mindset, simply savoring it once, you'll gain an exceptional gaming experience. But if, like me, you also aim to unlock every achievement, you'll inevitably find it tedious and monotonous.

The term “limbo” originates from Latin, meaning “the edge of hell.” It's a religiously charged term referring to the liminal state where the souls of virtuous non-Christians or unbaptized individuals reside—a transitional realm. Souls in limbo cannot ascend to heaven nor descend to hell, doomed to wait eternally at hell's border for redemption.

To find his sister, the boy traverses a long journey, crossing desolate wildernesses, leaping over deep ravines, evading deadly traps, and navigating intricate mechanisms. He pushes through the edge of life and death to see her. At the end, he breaks through the boundaries of LIMBO and glimpses her silhouette. Yet no one knows whether the girl's face, when she turns, bears the grimace of the realm of death or the joy of a family reunion. That boy, throughout his long journey, escaped one deadly peril after another, running relentlessly without pause or fear. But in that final moment, when he glimpsed her silhouette, his steps slowed, becoming hesitant and uncertain. Finally, he stopped. The game abruptly ended at that moment. After the credits rolled, all that remained were two corpses and the flies circling above them.

I believe different players will interpret the game's narrative and its ending in distinct ways. Perhaps you felt overwhelming despair and emptiness, or maybe you sensed a glimmer of hope and beauty. Regardless, LIMBO undeniably showcases exceptional atmospheric design and narrative through its environment.

However, from a gameplay perspective, LIMBO's controls feel clunky and unresponsive. Some puzzle mechanics lack novelty or enjoyment, with low tolerance for error. Combined with its deliberate pace, this can lead to frustration.

Particularly notable is an achievement requiring completion with no more than five deaths. This demands starting a new game and playing through without quitting or loading chapters—a single, uninterrupted run with fewer than five deaths to unlock. I swear this achievement ranks among the most frustrating and exhausting ones I've earned this year. For a game like LIMBO, which sells itself on its atmospheric experience, coupled with its already poor controls, approaching it with such a rigid objective completely shifts your mindset. That intense, nerve-wracking feeling instantly takes over. If you make a mistake during the run and exceed five deaths—even if you're just moments away from finishing—you have to start the entire game over. At that point, the game becomes incredibly frustrating. Fortunately, I had played LIMBO over a decade ago (on a mobile platform back then) and got lucky enough to finally complete this achievement.

In summary, LIMBO is undoubtedly an exceptional game. For first-time players, I recommend approaching it with a mindset focused on experiencing the story and atmosphere—this will yield the most satisfying overall experience. But if you aim to unlock every achievement, brace yourself for a challenging journey.

LIMBO won me over because it turns a very simple structure into something memorable through atmosphere, pacing, and restraint. LIMBO is a puzzle platformer that never feels the need to explain too much, and that is exactly part of its strength. What stood out the most to me was its visual identity, with that black and white world, its oppressive mood, and puzzles that stay engaging without becoming overly complicated. It is a short game, and some sections rely on trial and error, but it uses both to its advantage instead of wasting your time. 

In my experience, it still feels like a piece of art that has aged remarkably well. I liked how it kept pulling me forward with almost no dialogue, just through curiosity, danger, and smart puzzle design. That said, it is better to go in knowing it is not a long game and that some deaths are part of learning how each section works. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys atmospheric games, light puzzles, and memorable visual design. Not so much for someone looking for a long adventure or a more direct and explained story.

A boy enters LIMBO...

In LIMBO, you play as a boy looking for his lost sister. The game begins with no explanation, and indeed the entire experience has absolutely no dialogue or exposition whatsoever - everything is left open to the player's interpretation. A side-scrolling 2D "platformer", LIMBO will have you overcoming obstacles and puzzles in pursuit of your lost sibling, and is sure to elicit some shock value due to some of the content (why are there dead kids?).

LIMBO is also proof that you do not need a big budget or fancy graphics to create a fantastic and immersive game - this is perhaps the definition of "atmospheric", thanks to wonderful use of a black and white world to draw you further into the gloom and confusion, and some of the best sound design I have ever heard in any game. There are so many tiny details added in which increases the illusion - the soft puffs of dust as the boy runs, the tiny patter of raindrops falling, etc.

This is not far off being an artform... highly recommended to anyone looking for an experience, rather than a distraction.

EDIT: Played on Windows 10 Pro x64 without any issues.

Much like every other aspect of the game varying from the simple controls and minimal story-telling to its short length, the B&W graphics are also very simplistic yet so eerily pretty, as if conveying the message that sometimes ”less is more”.

I would’ve hoped for a clearer insight into Limbo’s fascinating world as well as a more forgiving approach to the timed puzzles like in its follower INSIDE, but this surely is a thrilling experience for those who love a bit of horror-ish puzzling and cursing. I know, I’m sorry, Mom.

But first, an English lesson.  
Skill (noun) ~ the ability, coming from one's knowledge, practice, aptitude, etc., to do something well. Usage: "The dancers performed with skill."

Recollection (noun) ~ the act or power of recollecting, or recalling to mind; remembrance. Usage: "Bob had perfect recollection of everything he did wrong when crossing the street."

It's too bad that the developers of this game confused these two. There is apparently some underlying artistic expression happening in Limbo related to depression and suicide. So they sat down one day and figured the best way to express that was to just kill the player over and over again by making it impossible to progress without actually having fore-knowledge of what will happen next. Then they remembered that they were actually supposed to be making a game and threw in some puzzles, some of which were very clever but ultimately the result is that Limbo feels like it wants to be doing two very different things and can't make up its mind.

Schizophrenic design and a focus on the theme of depression... somehow they didn't think it was a bad idea on paper. I'll say this though, they certainly captured the essense of suicide. Because they completely killed any hope of this game being entertaining.

As a final note, the game is sickeningly violent. That may seem like an odd thing to say because the game is all greyscale but the fact is that the developers have intentionally gone to great lengths to make the main character's deaths as vivid as possible. The game repeatedly has the main character dismembered, bisected, beheaded, crushed and impaled all with gruesome detail both visually and aurally. You can hear the bones crunch and flesh tear as well as see and hear blood splatter. It isn't pleasent and it may be the singular reason for the high reviews as many see this kind of morbid stuff as highly entertaining. Furthermore if you are a parent looking to buy this for a child, thinking that it is harmless, you need to look elsewhere.

“Limbo” makes the absolute best of its bleak world painted in blacks and grays with an occasional white for a light source. I suppose if there is a limbo out there, it can very well look like this - very stylish and dark (literally and figuratively), minimalistic and yet somehow arresting at the same time. Who knew a protagonist who is basically a black shadow with white eyes could be so compelling? We navigate this nameless little boy with a bare minimum of commands – you can run, jump and push/pull (arrows + Ctrl). That’s it. Doesn’t sound like much but it appeared to be enough to kill the little guy many times over, so this very intuitive and smoothly integrated control system works perfect for all intended purposes.

What else works great is the abrupt beginning – we get up in the world of a game straight from the launch icon. No menus, no “starts”, no silliness all the other games bother with – just get up and walk. It does wonders for immersion in the story. What story? Well…That’s for a player to figure out. Up until the end (which was pretty vague in itself) I had no idea why I was going to wherever it is I was going. I have a maybe 0.19% better understanding now. Not much but, hey, that “going” was fun! The virtual absence of any kind of storyline/plot surprisingly does NOT makes this game any less fantastic, but if you’re looking for one – this isn’t the game. 

The puzzles are that of high quality, employing physics and timing and requiring brain cells and coordination combos to figure out, and because of that are an absolute pleasure to tackle. The progression is a bit unstable as they were of decent difficulty through a good 2/3rd of the game until a sudden ramp-up to a highest degree after which you go from figuring out a puzzle somewhat intuitively, after a few tries, to sitting there for good 30 minutes just trying to map out a right decision. I enjoyed the process but for those who rage quickly it might be frustrating; mostly because every time you go wrong little boy dies.  Sometimes you go wrong many times in a row and this child dies over and over and over the most brutal, gruesome, horrific, appalling deaths you can imagine. It’s especially fun on the first try – when it’s unexpected. Nothing quite like being suddenly squished by a platform now ascending with his guts sticking to it… Or a quick jump right onto rotating saw blade… The secret level is a special treat - you’re walking through obstacles in almost complete darkness, operating mostly by hearing. Let me correct my previous sentence – there’s nothing quite like jumping right onto rotating saw blade IN COMPLETE DARKNESS. Yes, now it sounds right.

“Limbo” might be on a shorter side, but it’s a work of art. It has macabre aesthetic for days, smart challenging puzzles and a very intuitive gameplay. Even if puzzle platformers aren’t your usual thing (they aren’t for me), this would be the one to have. After all, you come across only as many games where your character uses dead body as a prop.

A really excellent game. I picked this one up to play on the Steamdeck and I'm super happy with how it performs, it runs at a locked 90FPS without any audio, video or control issues, you boot it up and it works flawlessly. 

The game itself is about 45m long from start to finish, so about 60-90m if you're playing for the first time (expect lots of deaths while you learn the puzzles) 

There's two really brutal achievements here, I thought I'd outline them here in case anyone else wants to achievement hunt. 

1) Completing the hidden level, which you can only get by collecting all of the secret eggs in the game. This level is incredibly difficult, with most of the level being in pitch black, so you need to listen to audio cues for when you need to jump and run. You'll need a guide for this one because it's brutal. The only saving grace is when you die you don't start the level over again, you respawn close to where you died. 

2) Beating the game with a maximum of 5 deaths. This one was hands down one of the hardest achievements I've completed, even though the game is only 40m long you can die on dozens on traps, costing you a life. 

There's about 6 really difficult sections in the game where you need to play perfectly, with the end final jump being arguably the most difficult to master (and where I lost multiple runs )

Even though you can use the chapter select to play the difficult sections and practice, it's doing the run from start to finish thats a killer. It took about 8 hours for me to get this one but I'm super happy I stuck it out because it really tests your mastery of the game. 

There's a few full playthroughs and even a few deathless runs but you'll only get this one if you keep playing and master each of the tricky puzzles.

LIMBO is a 2D puzzle platformer. I haven't really paid much attention to the game and just got into it recently. It pays homage to games of old with it's simplistic style yet engaging content through it's simplicity.


Pros:
+ The controls are nice and feels intuitive. It's kinda fast paced but doesn't force you to do ridiculous jumps all the time like other platformers which make you rely solely on reaction time and memorizing routes though you might need to in order to finish the achievement of not dying more than 5 times in a single timed playthrough.

+ The soundtrack consists mostly of ambient noise and fragments of something that sounds like a song here and there. I enjoy it myself, being in this shadowy world that's completely in silence really helps to build up the atmosphere. Sometimes the music gets louder, sometimes it's in complete silence. Really takes you into an almost movie like setting.

+ Perhaps the thing I love the most about this game. The visuals; The whole world is black and white, with some kind of mist in the background. The characters are nothing but mere shadows, even the protagonist is a kid shrouded in shadows with just his eyes glowing. The world is gorgeous in a depressing way, after all, you're in Limbo. Forests, industrial areas, caves, lakes, even something that looks like a city. Rain pours down on you at some point, and it's nice and soothing. I really like the art style of this game. It's kinda gory too, your character can die in a wide array of painful deaths. Some are quite gory. Still, it's all in black and white, you'll see the shadows of your intestines. 

+ The world itself. This might count towards the visuals, though. This game is quite somber, and really atmospheric. You're adventuring into the unknown, and you'll find all kinds of weird stuff along the way. You'll find corpses all around, some of them suicide victims. Even the living beings in Limbo are hostile towards you. It truly is a cold and unforgiving world.

Neutral:

+/- This game gets quite challenging later on. This might be a con for some, a pro for others. Personally, I enjoy it myself. You simply can't finish this game without dying quite a few times on the first run, because the game changes its rules at times, teases you, punishes you for taking the "easy" route. Sometimes, deaths are swift and gory, with less than a second to react. This game is a lot of trial and error, just like you'd expect from a game like this.

-/+ Another pro for some, con for others. This game is quite short. Puzzles are time consuming, and I dare to say, frustrating often, especially near the end of the game. You can easily finish this game in a couple of hours. 

Cons:

- Lack of story. I won't tell you exactly what happens near the end, but you might not like it if you were expecting something amazing to happen. The journey was worth it for me, but the ending felt kinda weak.


TL;DR:
7.5/10
All in all, I would recommend picking this game up in a sale. If you are into puzzle/platformer games this is quite an interersting title, especially coming from an indie game. The visuals and ambience alone are worth it for me, and the game's short enough for me to avoid giving up in frustration before completing it.

I heard lots of great things about this game, so I decided to buy it at a discount along with INSIDE. The first hour was unlike anything I've ever played before. The pitch-black landscape and undisclosed identity of the main character wrap the game in a shroud of mystery, and I immediately wanted to find out more. Even after completion, the game doesn't reveal much. LIMBO succeeds in this respect, because it leaves much of the story up for interpretation and forces you to actually think(something not many games do at all). Similarly to how rich writing creates a certain vagueness, LIMBO's setting is what makes it so enigmatic. 

Another aspect of the game I enjoyed was how smoothly the different areas blended together. You begin in a forest, run into some natives, and before you know it, you are inside a factory. Though there is a rigid dichotomy between nature and industry, LIMBO blends these elements seamlessly, without any obnoxious loading screens.

Why do I not recommend this game? It begins to feel empty and boring very quickly. In the beginning, the puzzles involved ripping the legs off a giant spider, bringing an unprecedented sense of satisfaction. After this thrilling section of the game, the puzzles turned into mind-numbing block-pushing, button-pressing, and lever-activating. The fearsome giant spider was replaced by an annoying little maggot that burrows in your character's skull, causing him to move in one direction until you reach the spot where the game changes your direction for you. Though the idea is interesting, I always dreaded the moment when I would contract a brainworm and lose control of my character. 

The unfortunate truth is that the segment with bad puzzles constitutes the majority of the game experience. Even when LIMBO introduces a cool new gravity changing mechanic, the damn block-pushing puzzles are still there, and everything begins to feel like one big chore. I actually wanted the game to end. Luckily, it did, because the game is quite short. 

Since LIMBO relies on a very simple control scheme, it would make sense for the puzzles to be based solely on interactions with the environment. However, the developers definitely could have came up with something better than pushing blocks next to ledges, or timing button activations. In my opinion, this is what ruins the experience the most. 

I plan on playing INSIDE very soon, and I hope Playdead will be able to deliver a stunning experience from start to finish.

I've heard people rave about this game. I don't get it. I love puzzle games. I love atmospheric games. I like games that make you think. This game offers all three in a very mediocre package.
The puzzles are not intuitive. You'll die many times and you'll have things click after dying at least a few times in most situations. You won't feel satisfied from the experience, that you "figured it out" or it just clicked in your mind. You won't earn it. The solution will eventually fall in your lap by trial and error. There's also a lot of points where you scratch your head about the solution not because the puzzle is hard, but because the solution is so deeply obscured. For instance, there's a point in the game where you are sliding down and you jump off. You'll see a rope well after you've started falling and figure you aim for that. But a saw is in the way of the jump. So I thought you had to figure out the proper way to get that jump right. The solution? There's a button you're supposed to press and change your direction from it mid jump. Cool. Simple. Except the machine blends into the background and you'll never notice it without it being pointed out. I had to check a walkthrough to even see it and suddenly the rest of the puzzles after were very simple. It wasn't satisfying at all, especially knowing that there seems to be a solution hanging somewhere else (and would have been a lot more interesting than what happened after this). 
Atmosphere feels really solid. At first. Then it's kind of annoying. I admit at times I had some apprehension, but it was mostly coming into places that go pitch black. The effects are pretty neat, but I found myself more annoyed wanting to see what is going on. I can appreciate this is meant to be a design choice that adds a certain feel, so I can't fault the game for it. I personally don't care for it, but I will say that it does suit the feel that the game offers and others will probably enjoy it more than I did.
As you play, you go through a small variety of environments with different feel to them that makes you feel like you're building up to something. You feel like there's going to be event or theme wrap up, but they never come. And that itself is fine, allowing you to transition to another area without any fanfare which can add to the atmosphere. But that's the whole game. You're held in limbo waiting for any meaning. I won't ruin the ending, but it only adds to the frustration. It plays a wildly vague finish like there was some deep meaning behind it all, but you have absolutely nothing to insert the whole experience into. You just get that ending as if there was closure to a situation you never knew happened in the first place and no explanation what this closure is. Are vague endings bad? No! I love when an ending makes you question things about the story. Limbo's ending? You're left wondering what the ending has to do with the game at all and nothing to really think about.
Notice also that most people have about 3 hours of gameplay in the game. It's a short game. You can play through again and chase down achievements, but that's as close to replay value there is. And now that you know what's ahead, the puzzle aspect is gone.
I appreciate that this game is over a decade old now, but it must have been a painfully bad year for gaming if this got such massive praise. My guess is it was a genre buster at the time. For the current price listed, I can think of a whole range of games with a lot more content and overall better than Limbo. Again, save it for a deep sale.

LIMBO is a game that I first played upon its release in 2010, though I played it on my Xbox 360. Just a handful of years ago, I remember being very creeped out by the game's premise and dark world.

However, after replaying the game just now, I find that it was not that exciting. It seems that I look at LIMBO and other games differently than some years ago. I thought that the minimalist story of the game back then was some magic answer, as if it was free of criticism - especially with the ending of the game. But that is not quite right. While the set-up of the game is definitely eerie, this time around I seemed to have wanted more. LIMBO definitely could have had more to it.

The early part of the game gives you that weird feeling because there are other creatures and seemingly human beings in this place with you. But in the later part of the game, all of that vanishes, and it becomes nothing but boxes and water and saws and gravity. The disappearance of other life could have been done as a means to make you feel even worse about the place you are in, but it did not have such an effect. If anything, it just seems like the developers did not know what else to do with other life.

Environment-wise, the game's appearance and sound fit the overall idea. In fact, music does not exist at all, and you only hear your footsteps and random objects clashing around here and there. Fitting for the "dead" world that you are helplessly navigating. Darkness. Fog. Minimal light. The visuals also fit that bad realm of LIMBO.

While I am not necessarily saying that the game is bad, I was just not as impressed as I was when I first played it. I feel like the game is a one-time-go, and then it's not really good to return. I also think that it is easy for you to overrate it (as I did myself years ago), because of things like the black and white shadow artwork. People seem to just look at the game and because of the visuals, it is already pulling them in and ready to say that it is good.

As LIMBO is a game, the gameplay itself is actually not that amazing. The game is literally die-and-repeat-until-you-win. Most of the puzzles have hidden obstacles or traps which are not easy to tell until you run through the first time. It may seem funny at first, but is actually not that amazing once you find out that a lot of the challenge is simply that. You have to repeat until you understand how to get around something.

For instance (slight spoilers if you care about single-pass obstacles), one of the sillier examples is early in the game. You are running through an area and you see two sets of mini-platforms that look like buttons, each of which are sitting on top of panels and underneath giant weights. If you run onto the first panel, then the weight comes down and crushes you. So you must jump onto the mini-platform button, and then jump across to the regular floor again. Now, as you'll probably know where it's going from my context, the next panel and button are swapped. If you jump onto the second button, you get crushed again. So this time you must use the panel and jump over the button, avoiding it.

The developers did the above example as a means to simply trick you easily and add a little artificial time to the game, as you'll have to repeat getting around it - but you only do so once. And that is very common in this game, with you having to die here and there until you are able to know what is ahead of you, and what you need to use to stop yourself from dying. That is not necessarily a good design, in my opinion. It would be alright to happen a little bit, but not as often as it really does.

And you also have the amount of gameplay there is, which is very little. Despite having already played the game years ago, I did not really remember much of the puzzles and still died quite a bit. Even so, I was able to complete the game in about 2 hours or a bit less. There is not a tremendous amount of content in the game; and quite a few of the puzzles are meticulous in a bad way, meaning a good chunk of the 2 hours was repeating attempts to get past the same obstacles over and over.

Sadly, I did not have that much enjoyment, excitement, or feeling of accomplishment playing through LIMBO. While I still intend to try out Playdead's INSIDE game, I do not see myself returning to this one.

[i]Limbo[/i] is one of the older titles on Steam that fits into an atmospheric category unto itself. Like its name suggests, the game takes place in a liminal space of perpetual gloom and frustration. You play as a little shadow-child, continuously attempting to move forward (and more often than not, backward) toward a goal that can only be described as the end of the game. Originally I had purchased this title here only to shortly after obtain it for free on the PS3, which concreted that this title is designed to be played with a controller, and any person willing to attempt this on keyboard should be marked as the sociopaths they happen to be.

Because of how simplistic this game is, I feel it would be a disservice to break this game down too much, as it is on one hand bloody beautiful and on the other, one of the most frustrating experiences of my life. The majority of the game cycles between moments of platforming and expertly timed puzzles. While the puzzles don't tend to be incredibly difficult to solve, getting the right groove to finish each puzzle is a bit of a chore. Thankfully, the developers had enough forethought to give decently placed checkpoints before and after each puzzle. That doesn't take the frustration of attempting the same thing repeatedly with minimal change in results, but it does mean you aren't force to repeat multiple puzzles to reach the same issue you have been contemplating destroying your monitor over.

At the end of all this I can honestly say that I came for the atmosphere that [i]Limbo[/i] offers, and stayed because it felt incredibly selfish not to honor the memory of the giant spider I shamelessly dismembered in the name of progress. After all, the spider was polite compared to some of the horrors that await anyone willing to delve into this title.

There is something wholesome in playing a game that so actively uses failure (and death) to actually improve your skills relatively quickly. It tickles parts of my brain that I don't normally use and it's very satisfying to get through the sections and unlock the achievements because the game wants you to pay attention to the details and use your whole range logic capacity. For someone with ADHD as myself this is also a very good engaging and dopamine inducing activity.
